intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that MEHMO syndrome (MEHMO) is caused by hemizygous mutation in the EIF2S3 gene (300161) on chromosome Xp22.11.

paragraphs.text: MEHMO syndrome is an X-linked intellectual disability syndrome. Its name comes from its cardinal features: mental retardation, epileptic seizures, hypogonadism and hypogenitalism, microcephaly, and obesity (Steinmuller et al., 1998; DeLozier-Blanchet et al., 1999). In the family originally described, affected patients lived for less than 2 years (Steinmuller et al., 1998).

paragraphs.text: Delozier-Blanchet et al. (1989) described 2 brothers with a severe syndrome of postnatal growth retardation and mental retardation. Features included extreme microcephaly, obesity developing during infancy, microgonadism, and a characteristic amphora-shaped facies. Neurologic examination was highly abnormal, showing hypertonia, hyperreflexia, nystagmus, and extremely irritable and agitated behavior. The first child died at 4.5 years of age; he had also had neonatal hypoglycemia and chronic constipation. The authors noted that the brothers most resembled patients with Borjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome (BFL). However, the dwarfism and mental retardation were much more severe than in any reported BFL patient, and the neurologic and dysmorphic features differed significantly. They considered 2 possibilities: a particularly severe, perhaps allelic, variant of BFL, or a previously undescribed disorder.

paragraphs.text: Borck et al. (2012) reported a family of Moroccan Jewish ancestry in the maternal line in which 3 males had an intellectual disability syndrome that appeared to be X-linked. Shared features were moderate to severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, short stature, and facial dysmorphism. Each affected individual also had features not seen in the others. Patient III:1 had cleft lip and palate and behavioral impairments. Patient III:2 had generalized seizures. Patient II:3 had postpubertal microgenitalism and obesity. Brain MRI of patient III:2 at 1 year of age showed microcephaly, a very thin corpus callosum, and mild enlargement and asymmetry of the lateral ventricles.

paragraphs.text: Skopkova et al. (2017) reported 4 families with MEHMO syndrome. Family 1 was Slovak and nonconsanguineous. In the index patient, microcephaly was detected prenatally at 28 weeks' gestation. Partial complex seizures were diagnosed at 4 months and did not respond to anticonvulsants. MEHMO was diagnosed at 10 months, based on microcephaly, seizures, hypogenitalism (micropenis and cryptorchidism), and severe mental and motor delay. Other findings included: - central obesity, short stature, and dysphagia - peripheral hypertonia with central hypotonia - dysmorphic features, including full cheeks, large ears, downturned corners of the mouth, epiblepharon, long eyelashes, thick eyebrows, tapered fingers, and talipes - delayed myelination, cerebral atrophy, and a thin corpus callosum - non-autoimmune diabetes mellitus treated with insulin from 10 months of age - panhypopituitarism and neonatal hypoglycemia - atrial septal defect, elevated liver enzymes, and severe combined dyslipidemia - recurrent bronchitis and bronchopneumonia - abnormal muscle mitochondria with decreased activity of respiratory complex II During intercurrent illness his condition worsened markedly, with more frequent seizures and poorer diabetes control. The authors noted that this resembled vanishing white matter disease.

paragraphs.text: The index patient of family 2 in the report of Skopkova et al. (2017) was the first child of nonconsanguineous Slovak parents. No other family members were known to be affected, and his mother was unaffected. He had low birth weight, microcephaly, and neonatal hypoglycemia. Seizures were diagnosed at 6 months; they did not respond to therapy and had no EEG correlate. Other findings were hypogenitalism, central obesity, short stature, hypotonia, partial hypopituitarism, and non-autoimmune diabetes mellitus treated with insulin from 10 months of age. Brain imaging showed delayed myelination, cerebral atrophy, and a thin corpus callosum. His mental and motor delay was severe: at 2 years his development corresponded to the third month of life, and he had no voluntary movements or social interaction.

paragraphs.text: The index patient of family 4 in the report of Skopkova et al. (2017) was a boy of Northern European ancestry from the United States, born to nonconsanguineous parents and last examined at 4 years 7 months. He had microcephaly, hypospadias, cryptorchidism, and developmental delay. He had a long period of failure to thrive, followed by obesity with a BMI at the 97th centile. Other findings were short stature, central hypotonia with peripheral hypertonia and spasticity, chronic lung disease, dysphagia, delayed gastric emptying, grade 5 vesicoureteral reflux, and congenital scoliosis. He had no epileptic seizures and no diabetes, and his EEG was normal.

The variant was absent from: - 188 X chromosomes from Moroccan Jewish controls - dbSNP132 - the 1000 Genomes data - more than 8,000 alleles in the NHLBI Exome Sequencing Project Ile222 lies in the GTP-binding domain and is strictly conserved in animals. Borck et al. (2012) expressed tagged I222T eIF2-gamma in HeLa cells. Much less eIF2-beta was pulled down with the mutant protein, whereas binding of eIF2-alpha was not impaired, indicating that the mutation disrupts formation of the eIF2 complex. The authors also discussed a p.V151L variant in EIF2S3 reported in an XLID family by an earlier large-scale resequencing project. The corresponding yeast mutation, V210L, caused defects in growth, GCN4 expression, and start site selection, and overexpression of tRNAi-Met suppressed these defects. The authors considered a causative role for this variant plausible.

paragraphs.text: Borck et al. (2012) studied 3 affected males from a family of Moroccan Jewish ancestry in the maternal line. They had moderate to severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, short stature, and facial dysmorphism. All 3 were hemizygous for a c.665T-C transition in the EIF2S3 gene, resulting in an ile222-to-thr (I222T) substitution in the GTP-binding domain. The mutation was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by capillary sequencing, and it cosegregated with the disorder in the family. It was absent from 188 X chromosomes from Moroccan Jewish controls and from public databases. In HeLa cells, the mutant protein bound much less eIF2-beta, whereas binding of eIF2-alpha was not impaired, indicating that the mutation disrupts formation of the eIF2 complex. In yeast, mutations at the corresponding residue (Val281) impaired eIF2-beta binding, derepressed GCN4 expression, and increased initiation at UUG codons.

paragraphs.text: Skopkova et al. (2017) identified the same hemizygous 4-bp deletion in the last exon of EIF2S3 (c.1394_1397delTCAA; Ile465SerfsTer4) in affected males from 3 families with full MEHMO syndrome. Two families were from Slovakia. The third was the German family originally reported by Steinmuller et al. (1998), in which carrier females were unaffected. The mutation cosegregated with the disease. Identity-by-descent analysis suggested a founder effect with distant relatedness. Truncated eIF2-gamma was produced in patient fibroblasts, and these cells showed increased DDIT3 transcript and CHOP protein. In a yeast/human chimera, the mutation impaired growth, increased GCN4 expression nearly 3-fold, and increased UUG/AUG initiation about 2-fold.
